name: Switzerland
description: Switzerland consistently ranks among the top countries globally for its high quality of life, robust economy, and political stability. It is a highly sought-after destination for expats, offering excellent infrastructure and stunning natural landscapes.
longdescription: Expat life in Switzerland is characterized by a high standard of living, world-class healthcare, and a strong job market. The country boasts low crime rates and efficient public services, making it a comfortable and secure place to reside. While it is known for being one of the most expensive countries globally, high average salaries often offset the cost of living. Switzerland is culturally diverse, with four national languages (German, French, Italian, and Romansh), and English is widely spoken in business and urban areas. The Swiss are generally regarded as polite, orderly, and respectful, though making friends can sometimes take time due to their reserved nature. The education system is exemplary, with strong bilingual and international schools available for expat families. The economy is robust, with low unemployment rates and significant opportunities in sectors like finance, pharma, IT, and engineering.

visas.name: Swiss B Permit for Startup Founders
visas.description: Swiss B Permit for entrepreneurs from outside the EU/EFTA who wish to establish and run a business in Switzerland, demonstrating economic benefit to the Swiss economy.

visas.name: Swiss B Permit (Lump-sum Taxation)
visas.description: Swiss B Permit for high-net-worth individuals who wish to reside in Switzerland without working, paying a negotiated annual lump-sum tax based on worldwide living expenses.

visas.name: Swiss B Permit for Retirees
visas.description: Swiss B Permit for retirees aged 55+ from outside the EU/EFTA who are financially independent and wish to reside in Switzerland without engaging in gainful employment.

visas.name: Swiss B Permit for Family Reunification
visas.description: Swiss B Permit allowing family members of Swiss citizens or existing B/C permit holders to live together in Switzerland, subject to accommodation and financial requirements.

visas.name: Swiss Student Residence Permit
visas.description: Swiss residence permit for non-EU/EFTA students enrolled in a Swiss university or higher education institution for the duration of their studies.

visas.name: Swiss Work Residence Permit
visas.description: Swiss residence permit for non-EU/EFTA nationals with employment in Switzerland.

Citizenship by Descent.desc: Switzerland adheres to the principle of *jus sanguinis* (right of blood). A child acquires Swiss citizenship automatically at birth if their mother or father is a Swiss citizen, regardless of the child's place of birth. If parents are unmarried, citizenship is acquired if the mother is Swiss, or if the Swiss father's paternity is legally established while the child is a minor (under 18). Children born abroad to at least one Swiss parent must be registered with Swiss authorities before age 25 to retain citizenship. Foreign minors adopted by a Swiss parent acquire Swiss citizenship if the adoption is full and finalized before the child turns 18.

Naturalization.desc:
- **Ordinary Naturalization**: This is the primary path for foreigners without family ties to Switzerland. It generally requires 10 years of legal residence in Switzerland, including permanent residence status (Permit C) at the time of application. Three of these 10 years must have been spent continuously in Switzerland during the five years immediately preceding the application. Years of residence between ages 8 and 18 count double, but a minimum of 6 actual years of residence is still required. Applicants must demonstrate language proficiency (B1 oral, A2 written in German, French, Italian, or Romansh), knowledge of Swiss customs and political systems, financial independence, and no criminal record or debt. Cantonal and communal residency requirements also apply, typically ranging from 2 to 5 years in the specific jurisdiction.
- **Simplified Naturalization for Third-Generation Foreign Nationals**: Children born in Switzerland whose parents were also born in Switzerland may qualify after five years of residence, provided they were born in Switzerland, hold a C permit, attended compulsory schooling for at least five years, are integrated, and apply before their 25th birthday.

Birthright.desc: Switzerland does **not** apply *jus soli* (birthright citizenship based on place of birth). Children born in Switzerland to foreign parents do not automatically acquire Swiss citizenship, even if they have lived their entire lives in the country.

Spouse and Family.desc:
- **Simplified Naturalization for Spouses of Swiss Citizens**: Foreign nationals married to Swiss citizens can apply for simplified naturalization. If residing in Switzerland, the marriage must have lasted at least 3 years, and the foreign spouse must have lived in Switzerland for a total of at least 5 years, with the year immediately preceding the application being continuous. If the Swiss spouse lives abroad, the marriage must have lasted at least 6 years, and the foreign spouse must demonstrate close ties with Switzerland. Applicants must also demonstrate integration into Swiss society and language proficiency.
- **Family Reunification**: B and C Permit holders can bring their spouses and children under 18 to Switzerland through family reunification, provided they demonstrate adequate housing and financial means.

tax_advice:
- **Three-Tier Tax System**: Switzerland levies income tax at federal, cantonal, and municipal levels.
- **Federal Income Tax**: The federal rate is progressive, up to 11.5% on income above CHF 895,900. For CHF 100,000 taxable income, the federal rate is approximately 4-5%.
- **Cantonal and Municipal Taxes**: These rates vary significantly by canton. For example, combined top rates can range from approximately 22% in Zug to 45% in Geneva.
- **Tax Residency**: Expats are considered tax residents if they move permanently, or stay a minimum of 30 consecutive days with gainful employment, or 90 consecutive days without gainful activity.
- **Withholding Tax (Quellensteuer)**: Most foreign employees with L or B permits and earning less than CHF 120,000 annually pay tax via withholding at source.
- **Mandatory Tax Return (NOV)**: If gross employment income exceeds CHF 120,000 per year, expats are required to file a full annual tax return (Nachträgliche ordentliche Veranlagung). This allows claiming additional deductions.
- **Ordinary Taxation**: C Permit holders and those married to Swiss citizens or C permit holders file an annual tax return for their worldwide income and assets.
- **Pillar 3a Contributions**: Contributions (up to CHF 7,056/year for employed in 2026) are fully deductible from federal, cantonal, and municipal taxable income, offering significant tax savings.
- **Pillar 2 (Pensionskasse) Buy-ins**: Voluntary contributions to cover 'contribution gaps' in pension funds are 100% tax-deductible, with a three-year blocking period on lump-sum withdrawals.
- **Lump-sum Taxation (Pauschalbesteuerung)**: Available for qualifying foreign nationals who don't work in Switzerland, taxing based on living expenses (typically 7x annual rent) rather than actual income or assets. This is not available in Zurich, Schaffhausen, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Basel-Landschaft, or Basel-Stadt.
- **Individual Taxation Reform**: Swiss voters approved a reform in March 2026, replacing joint taxation of married couples with mandatory individual taxation for all taxpayers, to be implemented by January 1, 2032.
local_tips:
- **Cost of Living**: Switzerland is one of the most expensive countries globally. Be prepared for high costs for housing, groceries, and transportation. Average monthly expenses for a single person can range from CHF 3,500 – CHF 5,500+, with Zurich and Geneva being particularly costly.
- **Language**: Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian, and Romansh. English is widely spoken, especially in major cities and business environments.
- **Safety**: Switzerland is consistently ranked among the safest countries globally, with very low crime rates.
- **Registration**: All foreign nationals staying over three months must register at their local residents' office (Einwohnerkontrolle/Gemeinde) within 14 days of arrival.
- **Health Insurance**: Mandatory private health insurance (KVG/LAMal) must be obtained within three months of arrival. Premiums vary by canton, age, and deductible, averaging CHF 300-500 per month for adults.
- **Residence Permits**: EU/EFTA nationals have simplified procedures, while non-EU/EFTA citizens generally require a confirmed job offer and face quotas. Permit L (short-term), Permit B (annual/temporary), and Permit C (permanent) are the main types.
- **Housing**: Renting can be challenging due to scarcity in cities like Zurich and Geneva. Expect to provide references, proof of income, and a security deposit typically equivalent to three months' rent.
- **Work-Life Balance**: Switzerland offers an excellent work-life balance with generally respected working hours and 4-5 weeks of holiday per year.
